## The idea

Play C major as C-E-G, then lift the low C above G. Both versions contain the
same three pitch classes, yet they do not carry the same weight. The second feels
lighter because E has become the bass. Harmonic identity can survive an octave
move while the chord's balance changes beneath it.

An *inversion* raises one or more low chord tones by an octave. A *voicing* is
the full choice of register and spacing for every tone. Root position places the
root in the bass, first inversion the third, and second inversion the fifth.
Those familiar keyboard shapes are also transformations of an ordered pitch
array, which makes them available for search rather than manual rearrangement.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78
use_synth :piano

define :invert do |notes, count|
  result = notes.sort
  count.times { result = result.drop(1) + [result[0] + 12] }
  result
end

define :distance do |left, right|
  left.zip(right).sum { |a, b| (a - b).abs }
end

define :voice_near do |notes, previous|
  candidates = (0..2).map { |turn| invert(notes, turn) }
  shifted = candidates.flat_map do |candidate|
    [-12, 0, 12].map { |shift| candidate.map { |pitch| pitch + shift } }
  end
  shifted.min_by { |candidate| distance(candidate, previous) }
end

c = chord(:c4, :major).to_a
[c, invert(c, 1), invert(c, 2), [48, 67, 76]].each do |voicing|
  play_chord voicing, release: 1.3
  sleep 2
end

roots = [:c4, :a3, :f3, :g3]
previous = c
roots.each do |root|
  raw = chord(root, :major).to_a
  chosen = voice_near(raw, previous)
  puts "#{root}: #{chosen} movement=#{distance(chosen, previous)}"
  play_chord chosen, release: 1.5
  sleep 2
  previous = chosen
end
```

The first three chords rotate C, E, and G through the bass while preserving the
pitch-class set. The fourth spreads the same harmony over more than two octaves,
opening a hole in the middle of the sound. In the progression, the search then
chooses nearby inversions so the parts remain in one register instead of
following every root through a large leap.

## Change one thing

1. Play `raw` instead of `chosen` in the progression. Follow the lowest note
   through both versions: the root-position sequence exposes larger leaps that
   the nearby voicings often avoid.
2. Remove `-12` and `12` from the shift list. With octave displacement excluded,
   the search has fewer legitimate neighbours and some transitions settle for
   more movement.
3. Replace `[48, 67, 76]` with `[60, 64, 67]`. Both reduce to the pitch classes
   of C major, but one stretches across a wide register and the other forms a
   compact cluster.

## Why it works

Inversion is a cyclic reorder with octave correction. Moving the lowest element
to the end is not enough, because the values would cease to ascend; adding twelve
places that pitch above its former neighbours. Each result retains the original
values modulo twelve, so the pitch-class identity remains intact.

Voicing introduces register as a separate choice. `voice_near` produces
candidates, measures their total semitone distance from the previous chord, and
selects the smallest score. This greedy search knows nothing about keyboard
style or harmonic function. It still removes conspicuous jumps because its cost
function makes one useful preference explicit: keep corresponding voices near
where they were.

That preference is incomplete. The least-moving candidate may put an unstable
tone in the bass, cross voices, or crowd them into an unhelpful range. Lesson 31
adds constraints for those cases. Here the deliberately small function exposes
the search mechanism and leaves room for musical judgement instead of treating
one number as a complete voicing rule.

The search is finite because the code permits only three octave placements for
each inversion. In principle, every pitch class has copies in infinitely many
registers. Instruments and arrangements impose practical ranges, so a real
voicer also needs upper and lower bounds. Encoding those bounds turns “keep the
chords nearby” into a reproducible problem with an inspectable candidate set.

## Take it further

Add a `bass_pitch_class` argument to `voice_near` and reject candidates whose
lowest note does not match it. Render C-F-G-C with C and F in root position, G
in first inversion, and the final C in second inversion. Print the movement
total for this constrained path beside the all-root-position baseline. The new
version should move less overall while still obeying every requested bass note.
